lines.trans: So the person with something from Grandfather turned out to be you all along, Rami.
Hello, Ziad. Thank you for coming today.
I recognised your neat handwriting on the postcard in two seconds.

words.gram: definite masculine singular noun, with عال- (on/at the)

lines.trans: Wait, you knew it was from me and came anyway?

words.gram: past, 2nd person masculine singular, with و- (and)

lines.trans: Of course I came. Why did you hide behind a mysterious note?
Because I was afraid you might still be upset. I missed you so much these three years.
Three years of stubbornness... honestly, little brother, I missed you too.
Excuse me, gentlemen, here is hot tea, and the lemon cake is on the way.

words.gram: definite feminine singular noun, with عال- (on/at the)

lines.trans: Lemon cake? Wait, how did she know about Friday lemon cake?
Sit down, Ziad, take off your heavy coat, and look at this blue suitcase.
Is that the old blue suitcase from Grandfather's workshop?
Take all the time you need, the courtyard is yours.

lines.trans: Goodbye!

meanings.note: Placed directly before an indefinite noun without ال- to mean 'the last' (آخر يوم 'the last day', آخر الساحة 'the far end of the courtyard').

examples.trans: The attic room is at the end of the floor.
Today is the last day of the week.

meanings.note: Takes a long -uu-/-oo- stem with possessive endings in Jordanian (أخوي my brother, أخوك your brother); dual أخوين.

examples.trans: My older brother lives in Amman.
The brothers sat together in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (باخد, بياخد).

examples.trans: Someone took my suitcase by mistake!
Old buildings take time to warm up.

meanings.note: The color blue.

examples.trans: The blue suitcase is in the luggage closet.
I have two blue teacups.

meanings.note: Polite Jordanian title for any man ('sir / Mr') as well as 'teacher' or 'professor'.

examples.trans: Please have a seat, sir.
Good morning, gentlemen.

meanings.note: Means something kept in trust for someone, and in Amman also names City Hall (أمانة عمان).

examples.trans: I have something entrusted for you from your grandfather.
We put the bag in the left-luggage closet.

meanings.note: First person singular pronoun.

examples.trans: I am Nour, the new receptionist.
I am Salma from the kitchen.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite noun أول means 'first' (أول يوم 'first day'); after a definite noun الأول / الأولى agrees in gender (الصفحة الأولى 'the first page'). Also used adverbially ('first').

examples.trans: Welcome on your first day of work!
Read the first page calmly.

meanings.note: Core Jordanian everyday verb for 'to come' (إجا / بيجي).

examples.trans: You came ten minutes early.
I will come on Friday at noon.

meanings.note: Used constantly in the polite phrase عن إذنك ('excuse me / with your permission').

examples.trans: Excuse me, may I pass?
He asked permission before heading out.

meanings.note: Introduces 'that'-clauses with pronoun suffixes (إنه 'that', إني 'that I', إنك 'that you', إنها 'that she/it') and appears in إن شاء الله ('if God wills').

examples.trans: Thank you for coming today.
Do you think that I am a hotel inspector?

meanings.note: Second person masculine singular pronoun.

examples.trans: Did you plant these herbs yourself?
Did you plan this entire meeting?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بشتاق, بيشتاق).

examples.trans: I missed you so much over these three years.
We missed our Friday gatherings.

meanings.note: The holy day in Islam and the weekend in Jordan.

examples.trans: The family gathers every Friday at noon.
On Friday the street is quiet.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بتخبى, بيتخبى).

examples.trans: Why did you hide behind a mysterious note?

examples.text: القطة تخبت تحت الطاولة من المطر.
examples.trans: The cat hid under the table from the rain.

تفضّل.gloss: to please come in / sit / go ahead / here you are

meanings.en: to please come in / sit / go ahead / here you are
meanings.note: Essential Jordanian hospitality verb used mostly in the imperative: تفضل (to a man), تفضلي (to a woman), تفضلوا (plural).

examples.trans: Please have a seat, ma'am!
Here you go, hot mint tea.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: تقيلة, plural: تقال).

examples.trans: This suitcase is very heavy today.
Take off your heavy coat and sit down to rest.

meanings.note: The standalone form of the number 3.

examples.trans: Three years was a long time.
One, two, three!

meanings.note: A unit of time or the feminine ordinal for second.

examples.trans: Wait one second, please.
He came back ten seconds later on the dot.

meanings.note: Extremely common Jordanian expression to express surprise or ask for confirmation, like 'really?' or 'seriously!'.

examples.trans: My grandfather's workshop was on this street.
Did you really finish all the work?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بخاف, بيخاف).

examples.text: مازن خاف طول الليل من التقييم!
examples.trans: Mazen worried all night about the review!
I was afraid your stubborn brother would stay home.

meanings.note: Can mean a physical line, a phone line, a bus route, or handwriting.

examples.trans: Your handwriting on the card is clear and neat.
Stay with me on the line a second.

meanings.note: Core word in خد راحتك / خدوا راحتكم ('make yourself at home / take your time').

examples.trans: Please sit down and make yourselves comfortable.
After the long trip he needs rest.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: زعلانة, plural: زعلانين).

examples.trans: A guest must not sit around upset.
Do not sit there upset, he will arrive soon.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: ساحات.

examples.trans: The courtyard has a big jasmine tree.
We sat drinking tea in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: سخنة, plural: سخنين).

examples.trans: Drink a glass of hot tea first.
Pour the hot water into the pot.

meanings.note: Core word in مع السلامة! ('goodbye!', literally 'with safety') and الحمد لله عالسلامة ('glad you arrived safely').

examples.trans: Goodbye, see you tomorrow!
Thank goodness for your safe arrival.

meanings.note: Everyday word for a year.

examples.trans: The building is eighty years old.
I have not seen him for three years.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: A staple beverage in Jordanian culture, typically served with mint or sage.

examples.trans: Please have a glass of hot mint tea.
There is black tea and coffee at breakfast.

meanings.note: Standard everyday 'thank you' across the Arabic-speaking world.

examples.trans: Thank you all very much!
Thank you for your patience, sir.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بشلح, بيشلح).

examples.trans: Take off your heavy coat and sit down.
He took off his wet shoes by the door.

meanings.note: Universal Jordanian/Levantine word (from Turkish çanta) for any handbag, backpack, or travel suitcase.

examples.trans: This blue suitcase is very heavy.
We set the suitcases beside the reception desk.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: صحاب.

examples.trans: Who is the owner of the blue suitcase?
We became friends from the first day.

meanings.note: Used constantly as بصراحة or bare صراحة ('honestly / to be frank').

examples.trans: Honestly, I loved the place very much.
Frankly, the coffee here is excellent.

meanings.note: Adjective used for size (small) or age (young), masculine singular.

examples.trans: We found a little wooden train in the bag.
There are two small streets on the left.

meanings.note: Warm, reassuring 'of course! / naturally!'.

examples.trans: Of course, Tariq, your secret is safe with us!
Of course I came when I got your card.

meanings.note: Used in عالطريق ('on the way') and طول الطريق ('all the way').

examples.trans: The hot tea is on the way right now!
I repeated the sentence all along the way.

طلع.gloss: to go up; go out; come out; turn out

meanings.en: to go up; go out; come out; turn out
meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بطلع, بيطلع).

examples.text: لفائف القرفة هلا طلعت من الفرن!
examples.trans: The cinnamon rolls just came out of the oven!
Go up the stairs to the third floor.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بعرف, بيعرف).

examples.trans: I recognized your neat handwriting in two seconds!
Do you know anyone here in Amman?

meanings.note: Means 'about' (عن الزبدة), 'off / away from' (عن جبيني), and appears in عن جد ('really!') and عن إذنك ('excuse me').

examples.trans: I will carry the suitcase up for you.
I heard your voices about the butter!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: Three years of stubbornness was too long.
Stubbornness solves no problems.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: غامضة, plural: غامضين).

examples.trans: Why did you leave a mysterious note on the door?
We finally found out who the mysterious guest is.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: قديمة, plural: قدام).

examples.trans: The courtyard has an old jasmine tree.
The old hardware shop is past the bridge.

meanings.note: Past tense verb meaning to sit down, or sometimes to stay/remain in a place.

examples.trans: Please have a seat in the courtyard under the tree.

examples.text: ضيفة غرفة أربعة رح تقعد كل الأسبوع.
examples.trans: Room four's guest will stay the whole week.

meanings.note: Past tense of 'to be' for 3rd person masculine singular. Widely used as an auxiliary verb.

examples.trans: How was the bus ride?

examples.text: تاني يوم ما رح يكون ممل!
examples.trans: The second day will not be boring!

meanings.note: Placed AFTER the adjective or verb it intensifies: تقيلة كتير ('very heavy'), شكرا كتير ('thank you very much').

examples.trans: The smell is so good!
This suitcase is very heavy today.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun; كرت بريد means 'postcard'. Plural: كروت.

examples.text: بعتتله كرت بريد قصير الأسبوع الماضي.
examples.trans: I sent him a short postcard last week.
I recognised his neat handwriting on the card right away.

meanings.note: Indispensable Levantine and Egyptian particle meaning 'also', 'too', or 'as well'.

examples.text: التفكير السريع أنقذ الفطور كمان مرة!
examples.trans: Quick thinking saved breakfast once again!
And I missed you too.

meanings.note: The main interrogative word for asking about manner or state.

examples.trans: How was the bus ride?
Tell me how to find the shop.

meanings.note: Refers to a single, whole cake, or a distinct slice (singulative form of kēk).

examples.text: كيكة الليمون الصفرا طلعت من الفرن.
examples.trans: The yellow lemon cake came out of the oven.
We sliced the cake into six equal pieces.

meanings.note: Attached prefix ل- before nouns ('for/to'); before pronoun suffixes in spoken Jordanian it takes the stem إل-: إلي ('for me / mine'), إلك ('for you / yours'), إله ('his'), إلها ('hers'), إلنا ('ours'), إلكم ('yours pl.').

examples.trans: The blue suitcase is mine.
Thank you all very much!

meanings.note: Takes pronoun suffixes in spoken Jordanian: لأني (because I), لأنك (because you), لأنه (because he/it — also general 'because'), لأنكم (because you pl.).

examples.text: لأنه القهوة الطيبة بتخلي الناس لطاف!
examples.trans: Because good coffee makes people pleasant!
Thank you because you kept the bag safe.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: لحظات.

examples.trans: Wait a moment, let me read the line.
We waited a moment by the gate.

meanings.note: Very common Jordanian word to indicate that an action is ongoing or hasn't happened yet.

examples.trans: Is your cup still intact?
Nobody has written anything yet.

meanings.note: The standard colloquial interrogative for 'why' in Jordanian Arabic.

examples.trans: Why did the person run off without his bag?
Why do you keep looking at the clock?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: ليمون.

examples.trans: The warm lemon cake is ready.
I squeezed half a lemon into the soup.

meanings.note: Used to describe a neat person, a well-organized room, or generally something of high quality (e.g. 'a nice car').

examples.trans: I recognized your neat handwriting right away.
Neat pencil sketches.

meanings.note: Friendly all-day Jordanian greeting usable with anyone.

examples.trans: Hello! You must be Nour.
Hello, Ziad, welcome!

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'with'; takes pronoun suffixes to express 'have on one's person' (معي 'I have with me', معك حق 'you are right').

examples.trans: You are right, Nour!
Goodbye! (lit. go with safety)

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: معاطف.

examples.trans: Take off your heavy coat and rest.
Hang the grey coat beside the door.

meanings.note: One of the most basic Arabic prepositions indicating origin.

examples.trans: I am Salma from the kitchen.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Everyday demonstrative pronoun for masculine singular objects.

examples.trans: Here we use this big ledger.
This suitcase is very heavy today.

meanings.note: Extremely common adverb used to express similarity or concluding a statement.

examples.trans: That is why the suitcase was heavy!
And after that, where do I go?

meanings.note: Very common spatial preposition in Jordanian Arabic.

examples.trans: Look in the mirror behind the desk.
The hardware shop is past the bridge.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: ورشات.

examples.trans: There is a brass lamp in my workshop downstairs.
The old bag is from my grandfather's workshop.

meanings.note: Collective noun used for paper material or leaves of a tree.

examples.trans: We use a paper ledger and a pencil.
He wrote a note on a small slip of paper.

meanings.note: Vocative particle used when addressing someone directly.

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Everyday conversational bridge introducing an inference ('so that means...'), clarification, or gentle pause ('I mean...').

examples.trans: So the house says hello by itself?
Does that mean there is no heating tonight?

meanings.note: Standard noun for day, often used in expressions like 'el-yom' (today).

examples.trans: Today the weather is sunny and warm in Amman.
Have a happy, successful day!
